translations.answer: High KD will directly convert joint velocity into damping torque, which can hold the arm but may damage the anti-jerk feeling. Verify the gravity model and friction first, then reduce KD and record tau/velocity/current in the limit/secure mode; handle structural load issues separately. The post does not provide final parameters.
translations.applicability: Not full-sized humanoid; 'first few angles' description is ambiguous.
translations.credibility.rationale: Environmental, processing steps, and results have engineering records, but formal cross-validation or independent replication is missing.
translations.details.attempts.0: Author used kp=0, small kd, and gravity compensation; comments discussed bringing J4 close to J3 to reduce load.
translations.details.diagnostics.0: Cross-verified from the main text, visible comments, and media; not independently validated by paper, source code, or official documentation.
translations.details.environments.0: 6-axis mechanical arm; MIT control; J2 kd=0.8, others ~0.1/0.
translations.details.limits.0: Not full-sized humanoid; 'first few angles' description is ambiguous.
translations.details.outcomes.0: No post-parameters test, no current/friction data.
translations.details.problem_statements.0: Gravity compensation holds the arm, but dragging is stiff; why can't KD be increased directly?
translations.details.safety_notes.0: Community candidate only for hypothesis formation; handle real machines with speed, force, and personnel isolation, and keep logs.
translations.details.suspected_causes.0: J2 kd too large, directly increasing speed damping; near-end joint load and model compensation error may force users to use high kd to dampen vibration.
translations.details.symptoms.0: Arm can hold, but J2/J3 damping feels strong and downward dragging is not smooth.
